opening_note: October is San Diego's second summer. Some years the hottest week lands now, when the wind turns and blows in from the desert. But the harvest has moved inland: new dates, new walnuts, heavy pomegranates, and a squash that will sit on your counter until Thanksgiving. For the first time since spring, you can shop for the month instead of the week.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

month_card.sub: What the desert and the valley send down.

field_notes.name: A new date isn't dried fruit.
field_notes.body: Most dates in the store were picked last fall and have been sitting since. The ones picked this fall are softer, glossier, and taste like caramel instead of candy — squeeze the box and they give. If you ever see yellow dates still on the branch, those are Barhis, eaten crunchy and fresh for a few weeks and nowhere else. Buy a branch.

field_notes.name: Taste the walnut before you buy the bag.
field_notes.body: A walnut that tastes bitter or smells like paint has gone rancid; the oil in it turns quickly. A new one is sweet and a little milky. Buy a pound when the new crop comes in, keep what you won't use this week in the freezer, and toast them in a dry pan for three minutes before they go into anything.

field_notes.name: Let the oven cut the kabocha.
field_notes.body: A kabocha is dense enough to be dangerous with a knife. Put it whole in a 400°F oven for ten minutes, or the microwave for three, and the skin softens enough to cut through safely. Don't peel it. Roasted, the skin goes tender and you eat all of it.

field_notes.name: October at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: Rockfish is the local fish that gets more reliable as the water cools: dozens of species, mild and firm, usually cheaper than anything flown in. Ask for it whole. A counter that sells it whole will scale and gut it for you, and a whole fish is easier to cook well than a fillet.

weekend_meal.name: Whole roasted rockfish, and the October salad.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In October, it's a whole local fish and a salad that only works this month: the first mild arugula, new walnuts, pomegranate, and Asian pear.
weekend_meal.card_line: Whole rockfish, arugula, pomegranate, walnuts, Asian pear, muhammara
ingredients: 1 whole rockfish, 2–3 lbs, scaled and gutted
Muhammara and good bread, for the table
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: No whole fish at your counter? Two pounds of rockfish fillets work too — roast them for ten to twelve minutes instead.
weekend_meal.method: Heat the oven to 450°F. Pat the fish dry inside and out and cut three shallow slashes on each side, down to the bone. Rub it all over with olive oil, salt it well, inside and out, and tuck the lemon slices into the cavity. Roast on a sheet pan for 20 to 25 minutes, until the flesh at the thickest part is opaque and pulls easily from the bone. While it roasts, toss the arugula, pear, pomegranate, and walnuts with olive oil, a squeeze of lemon, and salt — just before it goes to the table, not before. Bring the fish out whole. Lift the top fillet off with a spoon, pull out the spine, and serve the bottom fillet. Muhammara and bread on the side.

drink.name: Normal Heights Date Shake
drink.intro: One drink. It's still hot, and the dates just came in.
drink.card_line: New dates, cold milk, vanilla ice cream, salt
drink.method: Tear the dates into pieces and let them sit in half a cup of the milk for ten minutes to soften. Blend with another half cup of milk, two big scoops of vanilla ice cream, a few ice cubes, and a pinch of salt until it's thick and nearly smooth — a few flecks of date are the point. Drink it with a straw, outside, on the hottest afternoon of the week. The desert has been making these for a hundred years.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Go to the desert.
local_ritual.description: Anza-Borrego is two hours east and unbearable until now. October is the first month it isn't. Go for a day, walk until it gets hot, and notice that the dates, the pomegranates, and the citrus coming next all grow somewhere that looks like this — dry, bright, and irrigated. The season in this basket comes from inland, not from the coast.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The wind from the wrong direction.
one_thing_to_notice.body: A few times each fall the wind turns around and blows from the desert instead of the ocean. The air goes warm and very dry, the sky turns unusually clear, and from the coast you can suddenly see the mountains. It's why October can be hotter than August. When it happens, look east.

kabocha-squash.name: Kabocha squash
kabocha-squash.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, roasted beside anything
kabocha-squash.why_now: Kabocha is the squash that comes after the thin-skinned early ones — dense, dry, and sweeter than butternut, with a flavor somewhere near chestnut. It's picked now and actually improves after a few weeks on the counter, which makes it the first thing in the year you can buy in October and cook in November.
how_to_choose: Dark green, dull rather than shiny — shine means it was picked early
Heavy enough to surprise you
A dry, corky stem
A pale orange patch on one side is fine; that's where it sat on the ground
No soft spots anywhere
kabocha-squash.buy_this_much: 1 large, about 3 lbs. That's two trays of roasted wedges — most of a week of bowls and tacos.
kabocha-squash.price_note: Usually sold by the pound. Cheaper at Asian and Mexican markets than at most supermarkets.

kabocha-squash.weekend_use: A tray of dark-roasted wedges on the table beside the whole fish, for anyone who wants something warm next to the salad.
kabocha-squash.storage: Whole, somewhere cool and dry for up to two months — it gets sweeter over the first few weeks. Once cut, wrap it and refrigerate; use within five days.
kabocha-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Kabocha is drier than other squash, which is why it roasts so well: there's less water to steam off before the sugars can brown. That's also why it can taste chalky if undercooked. Roast it until a knife slides in with no resistance at all, then give it five more minutes.

pomegranates.name: Pomegranates
pomegranates.tile_uses: Over squash, salads, yogurt, the muhammara
pomegranates.why_now: California grows nearly all of the country's pomegranates, and the harvest runs from late September into November. In October they're heavy, cheap by the piece, and sold everywhere from the farmers market to the corner store. By spring, the only ones left are imported.
how_to_choose: Heavy for its size — weight is juice
Angular and a little lopsided, with flat faces; round ones aren't full yet
Deep red, leathery skin
A small dry crack is fine; a soft or damp spot is not
pomegranates.buy_this_much: 3. One pomegranate gives about a cup of seeds, which is a week of scattering.
pomegranates.price_note: Priced by the piece, so the heaviest one in the bin is the best deal.

pomegranates.weekend_use: Half a pomegranate's seeds in the October salad, next to the whole fish.
pomegranates.storage: Whole, in the fridge for a month or more. Seeded, five days in a covered container.
pomegranates.one_thing_to_learn: To seed one without a mess, score around the crown, pull the fruit apart into sections, and work the seeds loose in a bowl of water. The seeds sink and the white pith floats. Skim, drain, done.

fresh-dates.name: New-crop dates
fresh-dates.tile_uses: The drink, yogurt, a plate with cheese
fresh-dates.why_now: Nearly every Medjool in the country is grown in the desert two hours from here, in the Coachella and Bard valleys, and they're picked from late summer through October. The ones on shelves now are this year's — soft, glossy, and much better than the ones that have been sitting since last fall.
how_to_choose: Plump and glossy, with skin that clings to the fruit
Soft enough to dent with a thumb
No crystallized sugar on the surface — that's age
A packed-on date printed on the box, if there is one
Yellow dates still on the branch are Barhi: crunchy and fresh, and only around for a few weeks
fresh-dates.buy_this_much: 1 lb. They last for months in the fridge, so this is more about having them than using them up.
fresh-dates.price_note: Costco and Middle Eastern markets are often half the supermarket price for the same Medjools.

fresh-dates.weekend_use: A small plate of dates, walnuts, and a sharp cheese after the fish.
fresh-dates.storage: In the fridge in a closed container for up to six months, or the counter for a few weeks. Cold dates firm up; let them sit out before eating.
fresh-dates.one_thing_to_learn: A date is a fresh fruit that happens to dry well, not a dried fruit. Growers let them cure on the palm in the desert heat, which is why they're soft and sticky rather than leathery. Once you've eaten a new-crop Medjool, you'll notice the difference in the ones that aren't.

new-walnuts.name: New walnuts
new-walnuts.tile_uses: The muhammara, pasta, yogurt, the salad
new-walnuts.why_now: California grows almost every walnut sold in the United States, and the harvest runs from September into early November. Walnuts go rancid faster than most nuts, so the difference between this year's and last year's is not subtle: new ones are sweet and a little milky, with none of the bitterness people assume walnuts have.
how_to_choose: Pale gold halves; dark or gray ones are older
No oily, papery, or paint-like smell
Taste one if you can — it should be sweet
In-shell walnuts are heavy and don't rattle
Bulk bins that turn over fast beat bags that have sat
new-walnuts.buy_this_much: 1 lb of halves. A cup goes into the jar, the rest into everything else, and whatever is left into the freezer.
new-walnuts.price_note: Cheapest in the fall, right after harvest. In-shell costs less and keeps longer.

flavor_paths.name: Toasted

new-walnuts.weekend_use: Toasted and scattered over the October salad, still warm.
new-walnuts.storage: In the fridge for a few months, or the freezer for a year. Never in the pantry — the oils turn in weeks at room temperature.
new-walnuts.one_thing_to_learn: Toast every nut before you use it. It takes three minutes in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, and it's done when you can smell it from across the kitchen. It changes a walnut from waxy to crisp and from mild to deep, and it's the step people skip most.

arugula.name: Arugula
arugula.tile_uses: The salad, pasta, rice bowls, on top of anything
arugula.why_now: Arugula is a cool-weather green. In summer heat it bolts and turns harsh; planted in September, it's ready in October with a gentler, peppery bite. It's the first green in months that tastes like it wanted to grow.
how_to_choose: Bunches with small leaves are milder than big, deeply lobed ones
Perky leaves with no yellowing
No wet or slimy leaves at the bottom of the bag
Bunched arugula from a market usually tastes more of itself than the washed clamshells
arugula.buy_this_much: 2 bunches, or one big bag. Buy it twice a week if you can — it doesn't keep like the rest of this basket.
arugula.price_note: Farmers market bunches are often cheaper per ounce than clamshells, and taste better.

arugula.weekend_use: The base of the October salad: arugula, Asian pear, pomegranate, and walnuts, dressed at the last second.
arugula.storage: Unwashed, wrapped in a dry paper towel inside a bag, in the crisper. Three or four days. Wash it right before using.
arugula.one_thing_to_learn: Dress greens at the last possible moment. Salt pulls water out of leaves, and oil weighs them down, so a salad dressed ten minutes early is a wilted salad. Put everything in the bowl, carry it to the table, and toss it there.

asian-pears.name: Asian pears
asian-pears.tile_uses: Sliced raw, the salad, with cheese
asian-pears.why_now: California's Asian pear harvest runs from August into October, and the late varieties are the best of it. They're picked ripe and eaten crisp — unlike European pears, you don't wait for them to soften. They keep for weeks, which makes them October's lunchbox fruit.
how_to_choose: Firm all over; this pear is supposed to be hard
Heavy, which means juice
Fragrant at the stem end
Russeted brown or smooth yellow, depending on the variety — both are good
No soft spots; they bruise easily, which is why they come in foam sleeves
asian-pears.buy_this_much: 3–4. Enough for the salad and a few afternoons.
asian-pears.price_note: Expensive in a supermarket, often half that at Asian markets in Convoy.

asian-pears.storage: In the fridge, where they'll stay crisp for two or three weeks. Handle them gently; they bruise.
asian-pears.one_thing_to_learn: Some fruit is ripe when it softens, and some is ripe when it's picked. A European pear finishes ripening on your counter; an Asian pear is done when it comes off the tree, and waiting only makes it mealy. Knowing which is which saves a lot of fruit.
